utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you perhaps need just a few minutes to conclude your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have just one part of the video recording left to see. The last part relates to the 25th of May when the people described earlier were listed and buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you applying to have the video played?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The last video clip that we did not have the opportunity to see yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The same fast forward procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. We can see it. Not even -- it's not even necessary to see it all, just to see the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand no video has been submitted to the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was there the last day we worked. I don't know what could have happened to it in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, while that is being investigated, Mr. Milosevic, just carry on and we can return to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel. We have seen in video clips the events that took place in the correctional centre Dubrava from the 19th until and inclusive of the 25th of May, that is once we have seen the last part of the video recording. So bearing in mind all that we have seen and all that you were able to ascertain on the spot, because you were there on several occasions -- when were you there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited on the 19th of May, after the first bombing, and on the 25th of May. In the meantime, I also visited on the 21st of May after the on-site investigation team survived the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 21st of May is the day when you found the on-site investigation team in the section of the interior in Istok, the team that survived the bombing.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I saw them in a rather serious condition when they were at the section of the interior in Istok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in view of all that we have seen on the recording and all that you saw in those days, I will read out to you this entire paragraph 66(k), which reads: "On or about the 22nd of May, 1999 --" so the 22nd of May falls within this interval between the 19th and the 25th of May -- "... a uniformed person in the Dubrava prison complex announced from a watchtower that all prisoners were to gather their personal belongings and line up on the sports field of the prison complex for transfer to the prison in Nis, Serbia. Within a very short time, hundreds of prisoners had gathered at the sports field with bags of personal belongings and lined up in rows to await transport. Without warning, uniformed persons opened fire on the prisoners from the watchtower, from holes in the perimeter wall, and from gun emplacements beyond the wall. Many prisoners were killed outright and others wounded." Below that in subitem (i), it says: "On or about the 23rd of May, 1999, in the afternoon, forces of the FRY and Serbia threw grenades and shot into the drains, sewers, buildings and basements, killing and wounding many additional prisoners who had sought refuge in those locations after the events of the previous day. Altogether, approximately 50 prisoners were killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me tell you that it will not be appropriate to ask one general question in relation to these several allegations. There are many allegations in (k) and (i). So one general question will not be appropriate. You must address a specific allegation and get an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you were there on the 19th and the 21st or, rather, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days, was there a day or several days when investigations were attended by journalists?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of May, there were journalists attending the investigation, after the days when I was there. However, I read in the report made by the investigating judge that they also attended on other days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were you able to notice any holes in the wall from which somebody would have been able to fire?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about any execution having been organised at the prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were absolutely no stories about that and no mention of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those days, were there any units present at the prison complex apart from the prison guards?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 8, there is a description of this event. You saw at -- you saw on the videotape that, as you noted yourself the previous day, there were mattresses and blankets on the grass outside.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it would have been even better visible had we been able to see the recording at normal speed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it have happened that somebody would have called the prisoners outside to line up but also take their mattresses and blankets?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would not have been logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you have an explanation for the mattresses and the bedding?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the bombing, the prisoners slept outside, and it's normal that they took their bedding with them. It was warm, and even if it hadn't been warm, it is certain that they would have preferred to sleep outside rather than in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript that we received accompanying the recording, since we were not able to see -- or, rather, to hear the running commentary on the recording which is part of the investigative material, on that recording one is able to hear a voice, a voice that I will quote. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not translated. We haven't heard it at a speed that we can hear. I don't know how the Chamber wants to deal with it. This is again the accused giving evidence himself of what he says is on a tape that is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, we received the transcript in B/C/S, which hasn't been translated. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you see the problem? We have not heard this running commentary of the recording, and you're now seeking to make reference to that. Perhaps if you could identify it in the B/C/S version we could have it translated. Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, since the entire recording has been exhibited, everyone is able to check whether the running commentary is indeed on the tape. It was transcribed from the tape and the tape is in your possession here. I cannot tell you the exact minute and second on the recording where any of these quotations can be found, but it can always be checked subsequently. I can quote from what was transcribed on this tape where you can hear a voice. This is not a commentary made by anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can ask the witness, since he was able to both see and hear the recording, if he had noticed that there is a running commentary.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The scene-of-crime officers described what they saw during the recording. Among other things, they described the way in which doors were forced open, broken from the inside, so that inmates could leave the premises. And while we were watching the recording in the previous days, I made a remark that we were missing important details. From the recording we can see this and we can hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, does it mean that you cannot locate the relevant passage from this transcription in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can locate it in the transcript. Of course I can. I'm just saying that I cannot say now to the A/V booth where it is on the tape. On the transcript of course I can find it. It's in the last paragraph. And it can always be compared and checked. Here it is in the transcript. The last paragraph on the first page of the transcript. It says: "Traces on the door of the room indicate the way in which inmates forced open the door in order to leave the room, just like with the room across the hallway. For the main part, every dormitory within the building that had been hit was forced and broken by the inmates from the inside. In front of dormitory 35D, which held four convicts, there was a security lock which looks this way after the inmates broke the door open in order to save themselves and run away. Upstairs, at dormitory 33D, there is also a lock forced open from the inside. The place where the security lock was is just outside the door, and we are showing exactly in which condition it is. These are metal bars, probably the legs of beds, used as levers to force open and break the doors. This is the appearance of the door from the inside. "We are now in front of dormitory 54 holding convicts. They were not able to force the door open, which is why they broke through the wall." And then the recording shows this passage through which six prisoners ran out. And then they show how -- what the dormitory 54 looks like on the recording. "We see also broken bars from beds used during the breakthrough, as well as turned over mattresses, shattered glass, et cetera. Upstairs, also in front of the dormitory, we cannot establish exactly which dormitory it is, but we can see the door which were also thrown out of the doorway, which means the convicts acted from inside. We see traces of feet. In this dormitory we again see visible traces of disorder."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You can ask a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, after the airstrikes, did the prisoners from all these destroyed pavilions in the course of those days take any part of the inventory out? And here I mean, for example, blankets and the other things and place them on the grass outside?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left the premises and took out what they needed to survive out in the open; their blankets and mattresses and their own personal belongings. And they had time to do that, ample time, because the situation after the bombing at the correctional centre was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a reported account of someone else or is it an observation by the witness? I'm at a loss to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, what is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of this information is both videotapes and the on-site investigation and what the people who were there saw on the scene themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, in tab 8 in the report, which speaks about all the events in the Dubrava penal and correctional institution, does it also contain the observation that a number of inmates tried to flee?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That observation is included in the report as well, the attempted escape on the part of the prisoners, and that the prisoners were prevented in doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were attempts at escape but the prisoners were prevented, is that it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether anybody shot at the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information about that, and that wasn't the topic of my attention and investigation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could it have happened that in somebody -- if somebody tried to stop one of the prisoners escaping, that they might have shot at the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have happened, but it would be normal for something like that to be resorted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... disregard the rules. He's trying to give evidence. He's leading questions through this witness. It really, in my respectful submission, should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question is inappropriate. It's leading and just too inferential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you put the second page of tab 8 on the ELMO. I think it's the first paragraph as well on the B/C/S version. Could you take a look. Mr. Paponjak, while it is being put, I'll read out the passage for you. In this paragraph, you reported that: "In this attack, the prison perimeter wall was demolished in several places which enabled the inmates to escape from the Institution." You remember that? And then later, at the last sentence, it says like this: "A group of convicts attempted to escape; the Security Service, whose members had been deployed around the KPZ walls, took measures to prevent inmates from escaping." My question is what are those measures to prevent inmates from escaping? Do they include shooting at them and whether there were any casualties at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't write this report myself. It was compiled by the team that was appointed to do so by the Pec SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is signed by you. I don't understand your answer. This is a document which you signed, and you should be aware of these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. That is quite so, and that's what I wanted to say. As I said, the team investigated this, and that is normal procedure, there is a team to do that. And it is quite customary for me to sign the report and to become acquainted with its contents, of course. So I did sign it, but I didn't actually interview all those individuals and go into all the circumstances and the details of them. So if the prisoners did indeed try to escape, the security guards in the prison prevented that, and they prevent that pursuant to the rules and regulations. So quite normal -- it would be quite normal for them to resort to firearms and shoot if they couldn't prevent it otherwise. We didn't enter into the details as to how they prevented it, what measures they took, because that comes under the Ministry of Justice and not under the Ministry of Interior. It is their job to do that, the former. So in this report, we didn't write down all the details because we didn't go into all the details and investigate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, this is on a different note, but were you present at the place where the autopsy took place, and the place of the region is Rakosi cemetery, which should have taken place sometime in August 1999, for the victims of Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was present at that location on the 25th or the 26th of May, not in August 1999. I was there on the spot when the corpses were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I mean the -- the autopsy conducted by the Spanish forensic team. Are you aware of that autopsy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know that the autopsy was conducted, but I wasn't there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear about the results of that autopsy at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know what the results were of the autopsy conducted by the Spanish forensic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not hear that some 30 bodies had gunshot wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know about that fact. They didn't send us any findings, nor did we establish or ask for any cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before you go on, there is by this time a certain pattern in your examination-in-chief. When you're coming to the end, you either try to finish with a flourish or you ask questions which are really comments, which are more appropriate for you to use as comments when -- in your final address. So we inevitably come to a point of diminishing returns, and I think I see that setting in now. If you do not have any other pertinent questions to ask of this witness, I'm going to stop the examination-in-chief. There are matters on which you can address us in your final speech, but those are not matters on which the witness can help you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked questions that I assumed the witness could give me answers to, that's all. I asked the witness whether he had heard of anybody executing any of the prisoners in the Dubrava prison, and his answer was that he hadn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, just proceed. Proceed with the question. Let us now see if you have a pertinent question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, had an event like that taken place, that is to say that somebody had been executed in the Dubrava prison? Would you have had to have been informed about the incident?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly, yes. That kind of information would have had to have reached us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the tapes that we played, we could see some of the bodies and some of them were identified. We could also see some pieces of paper that were placed on the bodies. Does that refer to the people that were identified on the spot? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those pieces of paper, on the time recorded on the tape, 1.10, we have Januz Krasniqi from Prizren, for example.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does that name coincide with the list that you have in Schedule J, that is to say the one -- the list of the alleged casualties, those who fell victim of our forces in Dubrava allegedly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that list. I don't have that schedule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. It's in the middle of the list in Schedule J.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just not clear on one thing,

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: From your comments the previous working day, it would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. emerge that it would be up to me to prove that all the people listed in Schedule A [as interpreted] lost their lives during the bombing, and I think that Mr. Nice -- the burden should be on Mr. Nice to show that they had been killed as specified here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped that. I mean, it's a wholly inappropriate comment. I have never suggested that the burden is on you for anything in respect of this indictment. But to the extent that you're leading evidence, I have given you advice as to how that should be done best, and I have told you you can sit there and you can remain silent and say nothing in relation to the allegations and walk free at the end of this case. The burden is always on the Prosecution. It is mischievous of you to suggest that anybody in the Chamber has said otherwise. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just line up the facts that you testified about. Now, Colonel, how many prisoners did you say there were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thousand and four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in view of the description in paragraph (k) and (i), they were lined up at a gathering point, a collection point where they were executed. Now, what are the facts that cannot be refuted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That doesn't -- that's not a question to put, and you must know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. How many hundreds of prisoners, after the attack on the Dubrava prison, were evacuated to other prisons, specifically the prison at Lipjan?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all these events, about 750 prisoners were evacuated to the correctional centre at Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many prisoners were killed as a result of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how many prisoners were hospitalised, sent to different hospitals, including the hospital in Pec, Lipjan, and others, those who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that off the bat, but I do know that all those who were wounded and injured whom we came across there were transported to the Istok health centre and then to the Pec hospital where they were hospitalised. And I don't know how many there were in Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, gentlemen, according to what it says here, the description of the event that took place according to the indictment, it would emerge that the authorities had executed prisoners, and there were a thousand of those, 1.000, and then those prisoners whom they did not kill, who were wounded, they took to hospital, and the people who they did not wound were evacuated to other prisons. And the figure for those evacuees was 800. Can anybody imagine anything like that happening at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That has to be reformulated. We are coming to the end now, Mr. Milosevic. One more question like that and I'm going to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't follow, Mr. Milosevic, when you referred to tab -- no, recording 1.10 referring to one of the victims, Krasniqi, Januz Krasniqi, what 1.10 meant. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it wasn't recorded properly. It says 1.19.10, which means the minutes, the minutes on the tape, the time on the tape where that person who -- that killed person can be seen with his name recorded, because a piece of paper was placed on the body with his name. So that's the time that is shown on the tape. It is 1.19.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, I think we should see the record. It's one of the victims of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case my observation is of value, I entirely agree with His Honour Judge Kwon, and it's quite possible that in cross-examination I will be taking the Court to one or two passages of this video for my own reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to mention ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Following on Judge Kwon's suggestion, I'll ask for the tape to be played at the point of 1 hour, 19 minutes, and 10 seconds. That may take some time to prepare. While that is in preparation, Mr. Milosevic, if you have another question, ask it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read out -- actually, can I just say something before that? On the tape, this can be seen, a few persons who had been identified, and there are pieces of paper on those persons, and I have the exact minute reference as to where these bodies are. Januz Krasniqi is one of them, and that corresponds with Schedule J. The others do not, but they had also been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, as to Krasniqi, I think that the time reference the accused has given may be wrong. It's 1.17 -- I think 1.17 and 49. 1 hour, 17 minutes, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Will the booth first try 1.17.49. If that's not right, then we'll go to 1.19.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it on Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it is on Sanction, but I think that's Ms. Dicklich playing it. I'm quite happy to put it on Sanction if the Chamber is happy to see it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we play it back so we can see the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Januz Krasniqi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is where we started the clip initially and it ran on. Your Honour may have missed this. This was the first couple frames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be a different body but this is what we were trying to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, Mr. Robinson, that the technical people do have the tape now. Could they please play the 25th and the 26th of May now, that video footage. Perhaps it can be fast forwarded in order to see what was done with the casualties at the Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that may be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is to be done in the fast forward mode.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The voices can be heard here, the investigator dictating what can be found on the body for the purposes for identification. For example, he says blue trousers, black shirt, shoes, and so on. That is important for identification purposes. Numbers are affixed on everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is to be fast forwarded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move on to the next one immediately where they are buried, because this way it goes all the way up to number 93, so that will take awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, from number 1 through 93 -- actually, you've viewed this tape, have you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many numbers are there on these corpses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On orders from the investigating judge, the corpses were processed from the point of -- from a criminal technical point of view in the village of Rakos on the 25th and on the 26th. So two days. There was a total of 93 corpses. They were photographed, they were videotaped, all their characteristics were described, they were fingerprinted with a view to further identification, and then they were buried at that locality. The graves were marked with the same numbers that were used when the corpses were photographed. This went on for two days. I was there, as I already mentioned in response to His Honour Judge Kwon's question. So on the 25th or on the 26th of Nay, I was there and I'm fully familiar with what happened then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In tab 46.4 are there photographs of all the casualties? And further on in the same tab are there the fingerprints that you referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the criminal technical documentation of SUP Pec, what was done on the spot that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to read something else to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Professor Rakic looked at Mr. Nice's material and extracted a sheet of paper from it, and their number is ERN 03030807. That is a conclusion. It says "[Seal] Ministry of Justice." I assume since it says down here "Signed Dr. D. Emilio Perez Pujol," I assume those are the findings of the Spanish experts. I would like to draw your attention to the following: The date is the 3rd of June, 2000. That is to say 13 months later. In the document it says: "[In English] The cadavers from the Rakosh cemetery that were inspected match the following characteristics: "1. All are male. "2. They are between 18 and 60 years of age. "3. Regarding causes of death, it can be concluded that 45 deaths occurred as a result of the use of weapons from aerial bombardment, and 53 deaths occurred as a result of weapons or munitions used to contain or suppress the escape attempts."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, on the basis of this analysis that was made, could it have been established whether all of these persons were prisoners from Dubrava and whether they were killed in their attempt to flee, part of them, or whether they were killed during the aerial bombing? This happened a few months after their burial.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on the basis of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is another question that the witness is not able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the document -- and I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich for her speedy retrieval of detail -- I think that the document to which the accused has been referring may be Exhibit 165 tab 7 but that comes from, obviously, our electronic records at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, on the basis of what you saw yourself and what you saw on the videotapes, was a single corpse found at this collection point on the concrete runway where the prisoners were lined up?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They were all found on the grass or in the dormitories or in the facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'm not going to put any other questions to you regarding Dubrava. There is yet another incident involving loss of life which is not mentioned here in your brief, but it is mentioned in this indictment. Actually, in paragraph 66(f), it says: "On or about the 26th of March 1999, in the morning hours, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the village of Padaliste (Istok municipality). As the forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village, they fired on houses and on villagers who attempted to flee. Eight members of the Beke Imeraj family were forced from their home and were killed in front of their house. Other residents of Padaliste were killed at their homes and in a streambed near the village. Altogether, forces of the FRY and Serbia killed approximately 20 Kosovo Albanians from Padaliste. (Those persons killed who are known by name are set forth in Schedule E...)" Let me just find Schedule E. Yes. Since Padaliste is in the Istok municipality, it would have to be in the territory of your SUP, Colonel. Are you aware of this event from the area of responsibility of your SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I have to say that Padaliste does not exist in the territory of the municipality of Istok. There is no such locality there or within the area of responsibility of my SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But it says here that it was the village of Padaliste in the municipality of Istok that was attacked. Are you aware that a village like that does not exist in Istok municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure. I know that a locality called Padaliste does exist, but it doesn't belong to the municipality of Istok. It belongs to the municipality of Srbica. It is possible that we are talking about a halo effect. Everything that is bad has to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far would the one be from the other? The place where you say Padaliste is in the municipality of Srbica, would that be neighbouring the Istok municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes. It is a neighbouring municipality in terms of Istok, but it belongs to a different region of Kosovska Mitrovica. Had we had this information, we would have submitted it to the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, but we had no information about this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Am I right, Padaliste is in the middle between Istok and Srbica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, approximately, yes. It is by the road between Pec and Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you don't know anything about any such event in Padaliste -- it's my understanding that you don't know anything about anything that happened in Padaliste.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I'm not going to ask you anything about the village of Padaliste, although there were a few important questions in this regard. However, I hope that I will be able to put them to another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, can I ask you to have these exhibits admitted into evidence, those that I submitted along with this witness. We analysed in quite a bit of detail some of these binders. I assume that you bear in mind the fact that these are official documents only of the relevant authorities, and this is a witness who, from his official position, had insight into all of this and is testifying on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for various reasons I'd ask that the whole question of admitting any of these documents is reserved until the end of cross-examination. The principal objection at present would be the lack of translations of nearly all of them, but there may be other reasons for rejecting them in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll defer the decision, Mr. Milosevic, on their admission to the end of the cross-examination. So Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're looking at geography just because it may be helpful to have it in mind, as His Honour Judge Kwon says, Padaliste is broadly halfway between Istok and Srbica, but Dubrava is broadly halfway between Istok and Padaliste, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dubrava is not by the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean as the crow flies, it's roughly halfway between.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Put it on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 5. Further up a bit. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Up. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you should show the left part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, could I have the map back and I'll show you the bit I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was too enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court's got its maps, I'm not going to take time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that we can see Srbica to the right, Istok to the left, Padaliste just to the right of centre, and then just to the left of centre, in a diamond shape shading, we can see Dubrava prison. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to the right of that Susica, to which we may return for other reasons later. The reason I mention that Dubrava prison is halfway between Istok and Padaliste is this: You haven't mentioned it, and I'm going to deal with Dubrava later, probably now tomorrow, but the very witness who described the killing of her family in front of her eyes coming from Padaliste, Witness Lirij Imeraj, was also able to tell us about the air base that operated at Dubrava prison, because you can see from this map it's not very far away. It's right, isn't it, and you haven't told us a word about this, that there was a military function operating beside or at Dubrava prison, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that -- that it was actually a misunderstanding by NATO. The terrorists must have misinformed NATO about this alleged air base operating from the Dubrava prison and the NATO did the dirty work for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to invite the Chamber to cut you short whenever you start commenting. Just yes or no, and we'll come back to it with other material later: There were military functions performed at or from the area of Dubrava prison in the period leading up to the bombing. Mrs. Imeraj from Padaliste, whose mind was later much more concentrated on the loss of nearly her entire family, saw it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a comment. Shall we establish whether the prison was a NATO target in the sense that it was a military function or is it nearby that there is some place where there's a military function? Let's get it clear exactly what we should be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Nice, avoid the comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Paponjak, was it near or at the prison that there was a military function?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which military installation you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it your evidence that there was no military function performed at or near the prison at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that. I assert, I affirm that in the correctional facility of Dubrava there was no military installation whatsoever, neither was there one in the immediate vicinity of the Dubrava prison. However, during the bombing there were military positions that were a couple of kilometres away from the Dubrava prison. That is, trenches, positions occupied by the army, and shelters and covers, but there was no military installation or military function inside or in the vicinity of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the 21st of May of 1999, when was your most recent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. visit to Dubrava prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I never visited the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 21st of May your first ever visit to that area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. My first visit was on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your first ever visit --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st I wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 19th of May, your first ever visit to that area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the correctional facility of Dubrava, yes, it was my first visit. I went to places around or in the vicinity of the prison before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from military presence in the area, was there any special MUP presence in the area of Dubrava to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Dubrava, there was the presence of patrols, police patrols, that went about their usual business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to try and deal with matters chronologically and shall thus return to Dubrava later, but I want you to help me a little bit with these documents you've provided before we go back in time to where we must start. Who gave the order that these documents should be produced? You said there was an instruction. Who gave the instruction?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a copy of the instruction with you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did it say? Tell us from memory.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about the methodology to be used in drafting this documentation and stipulating the procedure in which the documents would be compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as the methodology, it presumably instructed you to prepare the documents at all. I mean, you needed instruction before you prepared these documents, wouldn't you? What did it say about that? Why should these documents be prepared?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went into reasons why my superiors took certain decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let's --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the scope of the instructions you received? Was this to provide a comprehensive analysis of all criminal activity between certain dates, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time period was 1998 and 1999. Documents concerning the work of the police in Kosovo and Metohija over those two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was all, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you from memory now what exactly it said. It was a very comprehensive documentation specified by chapter, which chapters need to be included, what the headings should be, and the approximate time period. There are many more chapters than have been presented here. It's not a problem, however, to obtain this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the apparent purpose of this exercise that you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, we saved this documentation from the area. We transported it in various means of transport, whatever we could lay our hands on in the chaos that suddenly set in. We placed documentation in passenger vehicles, in vans, and took it to the town of Kragujevac in Sumadija. And the teams who were unloading this put it in storage places, in warehouses, without any order at all. You must have in mind this was the state of war. It was towards the end the war. And now we were facing the huge job of taking all this documentation from warehouses, sorting it, gathering in one place everything that was linked to one case and placing it in an envelope to form a case file. Then these case files had to be put into a certain order and processed in order, one by one. So everything that was available to us concerning one case -- to achieve what? To complete all the unfinished cases, to lay a groundwork for future work, because we reckoned we would continue to work. We had a lot of unsolved crimes. We were unable to work on them at all during the war, and we were counting on being able again to continue to work on these cases, to shed light on these unsolved crimes and close the files. So we started sorting out the documents even before we received the instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there, how many police officers and ancillary staff were there working in the Pec SUP in, say, December 1998? Very roughly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this piece of information. Because in December 1998 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us a clue; hundreds or thousands for the police officers and ancillary staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hundreds. Close to a thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In June 1999, you all quit the territory, and you moved to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. The interpreter made a slip of the tongue. They said June 1999. So the -- 1998. So the witness won't be able to answer you properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1999, we left the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You quit the territory and you become, as it were, a SUP in exile in Kragujevac. How many of the close to a thousand, if it was, remain as an exile SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In organisational terms, yes, but in working terms that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, presumably Kragujevac has its own MUP or SUP. It has its own police force. It doesn't need a thousand new recruits. So what happened to your exiled SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely why I said that organisationally those people stayed in the SUP of Pec but not in actual terms. They were actually employed in other Secretariats of the Interior within the republic, and the necessary number of workers were engaged in the secretariat in Kragujevac for the work that we continued to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've spoken of heads of department and so on helping you in the preparation of this report. With the active policemen distributed elsewhere, so we can have a picture, from June 1999 until 2002, roughly, how many people were working with you in the secretariat of this exiled MUP -- SUP, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number varied. It varied depending on current needs. At any moment, I was able to take any of my men from any Secretariat of the Interior and transfer him to Kragujevac before returning him to the secretariat from which I took him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many actually worked in this office of yours in the period 1999 to 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 30 to 100, depending on the needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from dealing with any individuals who might walk in with either historical or current complaints of crimes committed in the Pec SUP, did this 30 to 100 people have anything active to do apart from sorting through these old documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What crimes were they investigating, and how, because they couldn't go back to the territory.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On all the cases we had on record in our files in the outpost of the Secretariat of the Interior of Kragujevac, we received people from Kragujevac or from people who were currently in Pec but they resided in Serbia or in Montenegro. They came to be issued with passports, driving licenses, and other documents, which is all within the competence of Secretariats of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My men interviewed them and gathered information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what investigative -- what prospect was there of doing any investigative police station -- policework - you knew you weren't going back - as from June 1999? There was no prospect of doing investigative policework, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know for sure that we were not going back. I wasn't certain of that, and I'm still not certain that we wouldn't go back. We interviewed all people who came to Kragujevac about all sorts of subjects, and that was precisely the work of my policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have two more detailed questions on this general topic at the moment, and they are these: So we can understand the documents even though we can't read them because they're not translated, if we look at, say, tab 1.4 and find material -- I'll let the Chamber find it. Starting at 2. -- 1.4, at nearly -- towards the end of it, at number 262, we can see the first entry after June of 1999 in August, number 262. If we go on to look at the last one in this collection, which is 285, for September of 2001, what should we make of these entries? Because we can't read them. Are these simply people bringing complaints to you or is this you investigating matters that you'd learnt had happened in the territory of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what's your problem with this. This is our work that we were performing in keeping with our authority in Serbia. We were not doing anything illegal. We were putting on record all the incidents on our territory regardless of the fact that they happened subsequently. The incidents involved criminal acts and crimes. If something happened in 2001, does it mean that we're not allowed to put it on record?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it from that answer, which is my next of effectively three questions at this stage, do I take it from that answer that information from any source suggestive of crime in the area of Pec is something that you should have investigated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We record every information we get regardless of whether it is accurate or not. Then it's our job to check it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And information can come in a number of different ways, can't it? It can come from an individual who lays a complaint, or it can come from public information which suggests a crime needs investigating; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know perfectly well all the ways in which we are able to work. Are you questioning me about the methods of police work? As a Prosecutor, you should be aware of that. We have many ways in which we can get information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And I think you're confirming that it doesn't matter how the information comes in, it's your duty, whether before or after June of 1999, it's your duty to investigate it if you can.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's not precisely investigation; it is the preliminary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these documents produced at Kragujevac in May or thereabouts of 2002, did they have another function, a public relations function?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something I don't know. We did not present it to the public. I never expected that it would be presented to the public, because I deemed that unnecessary. It is, on the contrary, in our interest to keep this away from the public as far as we can because there are things contained in these documents that we would not like to leak out because they could become accessible to persons whom we are targeting, among other things, who are of interest to us, and that is why I would like this session, among other things, to be private.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the MUP had its own website on which it posted various reports, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these reports published on websites at some period since their production in May of 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something I don't know. I worked in very modest circumstances in my exile, as you called it, and I had no access to internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The format of these documents is fairly uniform; report and appendices generally. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could another purpose of these reports have been specifically to assist this accused in his trial? Because they were prepared in May 2002, well after the trial had started.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said more than once, I can only speculate. But, no, in fact it could not have been the purpose. This documentation was not drafted for the purposes of this Tribunal. It would be unfit for the purposes of the Tribunal. It was done for our purposes, the purposes of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Entirely independent of this trial, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, it is completely independent. And you can see from the documents themselves that they were not made for the purposes of this Tribunal because the underlying methodology is unfitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask something. Mr. Paponjak, I am having difficulty understanding the purpose of the documents, and I want to be clear about that. Am I correct in thinking that behind every one of these cases referred to in 1.4 that there will be a case file from which the details were taken to be put into this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. As I pointed out so many times, behind each of these cases that has a number, there is a case. It's in fact a dossier. We called it a case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has its own cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is the purpose of this document? If you have all -- if you've gone to all the hard work of finding all the case papers which had been spread over the countryside when you had to leave, why was it that this document was then compiled? Now, I think at the outset of your cross-examination you said you didn't know because you were not privy to the purpose of this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very practical and convenient to me, at least, that this was done in this particular way, because generally speaking, we always keep a -- called log of incidents in our service. We record every single piece of information that we receive in this log. Some of those logbooks were lost, some were destroyed. In this way, we made a journal of incidents divided by -- into subheadings, and we are able to work using it if something new comes to our attention. Maybe you have noticed, maybe you haven't, that we even ordered things in alphabetical order in order to be able to recover lists more easily, because all our secretariats worked in very modest conditions with very few premises, very few workers, and it would be very difficult in such circumstances to find a specific case file within a short time. In this way, we have a systematically ordered material where we can find a case file on a crime within a minute. If it is a crime where the injured party's an Albanian, we will be able to find it because we have the alphabetical list of injured parties. If we did not have this, we would need days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask two more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take, please, your tab 2.4, one of these several informations that you've signed. Would you just look at the first page for me. Just the first page. Now, the first page -- not the first page. There it is. There is a headline which is underlined. Could you just read it out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The information is not correct."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information is not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about forcible deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information about forcible deportation, please? Because you haven't identified it. We're going to have to go through this document with you in some detail later, but tell us now, what was the information that was not correct, Mr. Paponjak, or would you like to reconsider your answer as to whether this actually -- this document, at least, relates to this trial and was prepared for the purposes of this trial? You tell us. What information? Because you're dealing here, you see, with the allegations made in this trial. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: When I spoke about the methods in which the -- this documentation was compiled, I said that there were different chapters that are prescribed by methodology. You have A, which is the chapter on events resulting in deaths; and B -- if you interrupt me, you won't be clear on what this is about, because we have tried to explain on several occasions, or, rather, I have, what this is about but I was always interrupted. B is the chapter on crimes against Albanians. B asterisk is where the Serbs were victims. That's the methodology. And now under the DJ, we have forcible deportation. That's according to the methodology applied, and that's why we applied this method and compiled this kind of document. Otherwise, we had no knowledge of forcible deportation but it was our duty to compile or, rather, to write down what we had, the information we had, to set it out. So this is an assignment from the Ministry of the Interior by using the set methodology to present information about forcible deportation, and that's what we acted upon. And let me stress that I personally did not compile this report or this piece of information either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before with the Court's decision we break, if that's what we do, would you go to the last page of this document and read the annexure for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will that answer the question that hasn't been answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He haven't answered the question but this will, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows, we have to deal with things sometimes more swiftly than one would in other environments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to the last page of this document, please. Now, read out what the annexure was to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It says: "Response to point 7, or count 7, of The Hague indictment."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, and I'm going to suggest to you all of them, were probably designed to try and defend this accused because you were answering there, and you didn't tell us this, you were answering allegations in The Hague indictment, weren't you? Or trying to in this document 2.4.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what's it say in point 7 or count 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us -- we're going to take the break. We'll return to this in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, please, what was the attachment to tab 2.4?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably it was an attachment of some kind. I don't know what kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it? Let me just remind you so you can understand the importance of this. The accused took you through a large number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. passages of this document in order to establish that the things contained in the document were true. You now tell us that you didn't personally compile the report or this piece of information, but I want you to tell us what was the attachment that should be with this report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's a problem to find the attachment. Just now, off the top of my head, I can't say what the attachment contains. Probably it does contain something pertinent, but one would be able to find it in the documentation. It can be sought and found, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that documentation with you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did have, what I received and brought here with me I hope is here. I don't know, as I say, off the top of my head all the documents that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every report comes with attachments, and we've seen other reports coming with attachments. You'd expect the attachment to be there. This attachment refers to, apparently, point 7 in The Hague indictment, and we know that point 7 in the indictment about Kosovo is a short matter of history. It's not relevant. So the document that was attached would explain why the author of this document wrote what he did, and I want to know from you what it was. You can't tell us, can you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you, no, because I don't know, but quite certainly the attachment does exist, just as the other attachments exist which have not been supplied together with the rest of the documents. So every information or report contains a list of attachments which we don't have here, but they exist in the SUP of Pec. So I assume -- actually, I'm quite sure that that attachment is to be found over there but not here since it says attachment, and I can't speak off the top of my head about something that I can't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In translation you stressed that you personally didn't compile this report or this piece of information. In light of that, do you wish to disown this report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how can you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally compile any one of these pieces of information. I said somewhere along the lines that the head of the Secretariat of the Interior can be equated with a manager. So he doesn't compile any documents, he doesn't interview any individuals. That's not his job. He doesn't study any documents. All he does is sign documents in his official capacity as an official. Among other things, of course. He has other jobs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who compiled this information, 2.4?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained that too. All the information --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the name. Who compiled 2.4?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was compiled in 2000 and something. What year was it? 2002. I can't remember now who was the person who did it. And that wasn't the essential point for me then or now. They were my close associates, experts from each particular field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't speak to the contents of this document because it wasn't your knowledge -- it was compiled by someone else -- can you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the contents of this document in front of me, yes, I could, and I could tell you about the contents of the other document, too, were I to have it in front of me here now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how can you speak to the contents of the document? It was prepared by someone else. You can't name him. You can't tell us what his sources of information were. How can you speak to the contents of this document, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, following on from that logic, I wouldn't be able to speak about anything here, because not a single job, the specific tasks, were something that I did. I couldn't speak of the work of the SUP at which -- at whose head I was because I didn't personally carry it out if you follow along from that kind of logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you can speak about one or two things that the SUP did, but at the moment I'm just focusing on the documents. None of the informations that we've looked at was prepared by you.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name the authors of any of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name you the team, the team working on this kind of thing, the entire team. It is teamwork. It is the result of teamwork, not the result of an individual's work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even this document is not the reflection of observations or experience or knowledge of an individual but is some way a composite, a compilation of views, experience of a number of people. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only with respect to experience but based on the interviews, talks, the other documents and all other ways of gaining information, on the part of a number of people, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the chiefs of departments, sectors, commanders of police stations, and so on. So it was a team which, depending on the case, numbered between five and 15 members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people permanently working with you in the exiled SUP or were they distributed around the territory of Serbia and Montenegro, sending in their contributions by letter, telephone call, e-mail, whatever? How was it done?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people would come to the command post, forward command post if you'd like to call it, and they were withdrawn from the SUP for a period of time in order to complete their work, and then, having completed that work, they would go back to their original SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any records of their meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minutes and records. Now, minutes were not kept, if that's what you mean, but there were, of course, notes that were kept, or records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are they available to us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the working notes that each of us keeps during the course of our work, and if you should so request, they will be made accessible to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you can identify the team. Do you actually have -- I don't want to have a list of names at the moment because it will take some time, but you could name them all, could you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the next break, with the Court's leave, I'll ask you to write the names down on a piece of paper to save time. We'll now go back in time, Mr. Paponjak, if we can. You are a traffic policeman; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subject to things that happened in Kosovo after your move there, you'd always been a traffic policeman. Most recently, what, in Uzice in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever posted at Uzice in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your last posting in Serbia before you came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cacak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank and position there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My last position was head of the department for traffic safety and security. I don't think there was a rank there. There was -- the position had a name, and I was a higher inspector first class. That was my last post and position. I wasn't a traffic policeman throughout. Before that I worked in the SUP Cacak department as an inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with what sort of matters?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative and preventive matters, professional training, and the legality in the functioning of the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Operative and preventive matters. Does that include detective work, anti-terrorist work, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That includes the entire proceedings, operative and preventive, in the work of a police force generally. So that means if it is to prevent crime and to stop crime from taking place, if that's what you mean by detective work, then the answer would be yes. I was an inspector in the SUP, which comprises all these areas of activity within the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be concrete about it, had you ever been seen as the leading policeman investigating a murder, a domestic murder, in Serbia, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been the leading policeman to investigate a serious drugs offence in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been the leading policeman investigating a household burglary in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those kinds of things come under the criminal police jurisdiction. I didn't work on matters of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your evidence there may have been some uncertainty as to the date of your arrival at Pec. There was a reference to one year, but can you please tell me, what year did you actually arrive in Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, in the month of August. I was sent from Cacak to take up my duties there doing the same kind of work that I did in Cacak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any possibility that your deployment to Pec was earlier, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I wasn't deployed there previously, but I was in Pec before that date for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doing what?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I undertook different activities within the compiled police detachment and unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that doesn't help us very much. Was it traffic policework or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't traffic policework. It was the work of the police, the general purpose police force. I was a commander of a unit or units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before 1990 and 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that have anything to do with terrorism?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't view it as terrorism at the time, but there were violent demonstrations, and it had to do with things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even if you only arrived in 1992, you knew and know that nearly all the Kosovo Albanian policemen had been sacked in 1990 from the Pec police station, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had not been sacked. They left of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you there when you came in 1992, as it were, in replacement of a Kosovo Albanian policeman?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a replacement. It was a newly established department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't have a traffic police department before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having arrived at Pec, did you in the early 1990s go training in another country, or at least in another state?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With a detachment of men?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the deputy, one of three deputies, to Vlahovic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I arrived, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Ljubomir Mikulovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later was it Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later on it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the structure that Vlahovic had three people at your level answering to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had more than three people at my level answering to him who were subordinated to him and who reported to him.
