utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those people at your level, even if you didn't, go off for training in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my level, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh, at your level.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people at any lower level go off for training in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about my department, things about -- things that I know about. So nobody went from my department. Now, whether anybody went from any other department, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, you have been able to speak very generally about all activities of the SUP as a result of all your inquiries and the work of your team. Think back, please. Did people go from Pec SUP for training in Bosnia? Try and help us.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could speak about the general activities based on the fact that -- of what my team did later on, the kind of work it performed, and I was very interested in knowing about that work. Now, what happened during that period of time I don't know because I wasn't interested in knowing. I was interested in doing my own work. So it is for those reasons that I can't actually answer that and say whether there were or were not. I was primarily interested in work done by my department and to organise the work there as best as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of training being done, perhaps by Arkan or his men, for people from Pec, possibly in Amajlije, Bosnia, south of Bijeljina? Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've given an account covering the period of the 1990s where, unless I've missed it, the Albanian Kosovo -- the Kosovo Albanians did all things bad and the Serbs did almost nothing bad, did they, in the period of the 1990s leading up to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, then, if you didn't put it that way, what the Serbs did do against the Albanians in that period. Shall we start with the teachers. Were they dismissed because they wouldn't take loyalty oaths from their jobs? Because you spoke of the teachers.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke of category -- in categories; Serbs, Albanians, good guys, bad guys, in those categories. I always divided people according to how they work, how they behaved, and things like that. So anything -- if you try and put words in my mouth and say that I said that the Albanians were the bad guys, that's just not true. Now, why teachers were dismissed, if they were dismissed, I don't know. I can't say. My wife is a teacher, for instance. She worked in Kosovo and Metohija, and she worked both with Albanians and with Serbs alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at Exhibit 205. Have you got -- I'm afraid this is only in English, but we'll lay it on the overhead projector and I'll read out the short passages I want you to deal with. While it's coming to you I'm just going to give you one more opportunity to see if you can, in general terms, tell us, what did the Serbs do against the Albanians in the 1990s leading up to the conflict, that was bad, that was criminal, that was unacceptable to you? Tell us, what did they do? Mr. Paponjak, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, I see. I thought you were going to show me something first. What I can -- I can talk about what members of the traffic police did, if they did anything bad, because that was the subject of my interests. I cannot address other areas and say whether there were good things or bad things on either side for that matter. So if you have a piece of information by which members of the traffic police did something --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it really your evidence that you had no knowledge of the activities of policemen other than traffic police? Is that really your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can't say that I had no knowledge of any other activities. But even if I did have knowledge of those activities, I need not necessarily remember them or recollect them or speak in qualified terms about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may we take it that you have no knowledge of activities by Serb civilians that might have been reprehensible because you were but a traffic policeman? You weren't dealing with crime.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had no knowledge of the activities of paramilitaries who operated in the area of Pec, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of them having been active at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I'm going to come back to this when we deal with the exhibits later, but if that's your state of knowledge, then when you signed off all those documents in 2002, save and so far as the documents related to traffic police, you were in no position to underwrite or to guarantee the accuracy of those documents at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I wouldn't have been in a position to work with my people if I were not certain and didn't believe in the kind of work they were doing until it was established that they had been working contrary to the rules. But as far as I was concerned, I believed they were doing their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me restate my question with the addition of one other clause. When you signed off all those documents in 2002, save and so far as the documents related to traffic police, you were in no position from your own knowledge to underwrite or guarantee the accuracy of those documents at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my own personal knowledge, I could not. However, for the head of the Secretariat of the Interior to be able to find something, according to you, it would appear that he would have to check each and every detail out himself, to interview each criminal, to read through each of the documents. That would emerge from your question. Now, I say that I sign what the head of the crime police prepares, those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here we have a document before us that's a Human Rights Watch report, and this one comes from March of 1993, and I'm going to ask Mr. Nort to display the bottom of page 25 on the overhead projector and then to look at page 26. While he's finding that, as a matter of general knowledge, you knew in the 1990s international human rights organisations were deeply critical of the operations of the police and other bodies in Kosovo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me: Did nobody ever draw to your attention as a policeman, or even in 2002 when reviewing the work of other policemen, did nobody ever draw to your attention complaints of serious wrongdoings by the police in your territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2002, no one drew my attention to that. I don't know. There were different organisations but I wasn't following their work, what they wrote and what they were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at this passage, and I'll read it out. Not a very long passage. This is the -- under a heading that's "Police abuse of civilians in response to purported Albanian violence," and the passage reads: "For Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example, on July 4, 1993, a policeman was killed at the police checkpoint entering Pec. No one was arrested in connection with the incident. Serbian authorities claim that the death was the work of Albanian terrorists." Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that on the 4th of July, 1993, a policeman was killed in Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the report, which is based on interviews with people at the time, goes on to describe how the chairman of the Human Rights Council of Pec said he knew nothing of the incident but how what happened after that was that the police searched homes, detained, and interrogated, and beat suspected village leaders, beating at least 148 people. Now, this is your police area. Is it right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page. Page 26.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Paponjak, so that we can have a true flavour of Pec for the decade you've told us about, or nearly a decade, is it right that in response to perceived Albanian terrorism or otherwise the police force of which you were a member was violent in its dealing with civilians? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this case. I don't know that a policeman lost his life in Pec on the 4th of July, 1993, let alone all the rest that I heard from you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go on, please, Mr. Nort, to page 33. Because I want you to understand and to comment on publicly available material describing life in your town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't suppose you have a name for the policeman, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This particular policeman, I don't think I do from this source. If I can find it, I will. It comes from an interview held in October 1993. I may have it elsewhere, but I'll see if I can find it. It may actually be -- it's possible it's in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can look now, please, at page 33 under the -- the bottom of the page, Mr. Nort, where it deals with raids on Albanian shops and marketplaces. Now, traffic police are out in the town, aren't they? They see what's going on. Don't they, Mr. Paponjak? Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So here we have this: "Numerous Albanians throughout Kosovo reported police interference with their commercial establishments. In a typical scenario, police raid an Albanian store and demand all of the cash on hand. As Ismajl Kelmendi, an Albanian clerk in Pec explained..." and then there's a passage on the next page dealing with how on September the 6th members of state security came in and demanded money from him and beat him or hit him across the face, threatened to kill him and so on, to achieve that result. Is that the sort of thing that was happening from your police station?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pec is not a big town. Citizens know policemen well by name and surname. A citizen who gave this kind of statement would have had to state who it was that beat him up. I'm not aware of any such case. Even if such a case had happened, why would I have to be aware of it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must understand, please understand, Mr. Paponjak, that you've come in at the accused's invitation to cover the whole territory of Pec, all the crimes alleged there, and to give all the background, and so I'm just exploring what you know of what was published elsewhere. Shall we go to page 86, under the heading "Trial of four Albanians in Pec." It says that: "On the 1st of October, 1991 -" or that's a little bit before your arrival - "a group of 50 Albanians met in the house of Sadri Shala, near Klina, in the village of Dobra Voda." Several of the members of the national movement for the Republic of Kosovo. They dined and discussed the political situation. Two years later, police arrested four of the men, for several days tortured them, until they signed confessions, it was reported. Now, we can go into the trial in detail but we don't want to. It's available. Is that the sort of thing that happened in your police station and was reported on publicly by organisations like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't read such reports. I didn't have them in my hands. This is the first time I see any such thing, right over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, if such things happened, how it could possibly be kept from a really rather senior policeman like you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was kept away from me, that it was concealed. The first question is whether it happened at all, whether we have it recorded as an incident or not. All of this can be something that never happened or something that we did not know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 97, please, Mr. Nort. Let me make it quite clear as we move through these few, comparatively few, entries, the reality of life in Pec in the 1990s following the removal of Kosovo Albanian police officers and other developments, was that it was life under a police state and that you were part of that police state. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that if we look now at page 97, you would accept, wouldn't you, that the presence on any state of paramilitaries has a destabilising effect on the community because they can't be sure that they're going to be properly protected by the other organs of authorised violence, the police and the army. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that only as a particular way of looking at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this passage of this report on page 97 where it deals with paramilitaries elsewhere, and we'll see much more detail of paramilitaries later, but it says here: "Albanian human rights groups allege that the north-western city of Pec serves as one base for paramilitary groups. According to the LDK of Pec and members of the Human Rights Council of Peja, three kinds of army barracks exist in their city: one for regular police, one for regular army, and one for paramilitary troops." And an interviewed Albanian is recorded as saying: "There are so many Serbs with guns around here, in uniform, not in uniform, paramilitary, not paramilitary. It is impossible to tell who is who." Now, is this a rather more accurate picture of your town than the one you gave us over the last few days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. It's possible that they made such statements in order to justify the presence of their units that they had already established or were already training in the forests around towns. This is not correct, this kind of presence at that time, some kind of paramilitaries or parapolice or whatever, because we knew each other. I knew every policeman, and every policeman knew me. So it could not have been anyone in a police uniform or even a unit without us observing that. So these parapolicemen were only noticed by this Human Rights Watch source or whatever the name may be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, there were a large number of trials of policemen, weren't there? Hundreds and more.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about that in town, that a group of members of the so-called illegal MUP of the Republic of Kosovo were brought into custody. That is this parapolice that had been established. Parapolice of the Albanians but not of the Serbs. And it's possible that this statement refers to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were tried -- I think the investigating judge was who? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had no contact with such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Danica Marinkovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name Danica Marinkovic means something to me, but it has nothing to do with Pec. I first heard the name perhaps in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those policemen were given very long prison sentences for being members of the parallel police force, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of sentences they were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of them went to serve their sentences in Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just leaping forward for a second before we return to the place in the chronology, by the time of the bombing of Dubrava prison, it was very substantially occupied by political prisoners, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what "political prisoners" means in your books. The persons there were persons who were convicted of crimes, accused persons, or persons brought into custody on the suspicion that they had committed serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such crimes as gathering together to discuss politics, something like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anyone having been convicted for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit 188, please, which may help us get a few things in chronological perspective. Now, this is another report, this one again from Human Rights Watch. It's dated December 1996. But if we go first to page 16. Just about halfway down the page. And the year is 1996, so it's after the policemen trial. We see this: "On August 28, three grenades were thrown at the police station in Lolopak near Pec, causing no casualties but substantial material damage. That same day, an inspector with the Serbian police, Ejup Bajgora, was killed by automatic gunfire near his home in Lupc near Podujevo. Finally ... a Serbian police officer, Inspector Milos Nikic, and an employment office employee, Dragan Rakic, were ambushed and killed by unknown attackers in the village of Surkis near Podujevo. "Albanian leaders and Serbian officials both denied any involvement in the violence and accused the other side of provoking conflict. Meanwhile, a previously unknown organisation called the Kosovo Liberation Army claimed responsibility for the attacks." Pausing there. Do you remember the grenades thrown at that nearby police station?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There is no such a police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the deaths of Serb police colleagues at about this time in 1996?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were killings of policemen in 1996 and in 1997. I cannot give you the exact time of death of these colleagues, and it wasn't in my area either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the suggestion in this report that it's in 1996 that the words "Kosovo Liberation Army" first come to be used in an acknowledgement of gross violence and killings, does that accord with your recollection of the time scale?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was not involved in such things. I know that there were different groups that were called the Liberation Army, the People's Army. Their bases were at Cicavica and on the other mountains where the training took place. I don't know exactly when this term was first used, the Kosovo Liberation Army, because at that time I was not dealing with such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, even if you didn't read these reports at the time or have them drawn to your attention, you'll observe that this report covers violence done by Kosovo Albanians to Serbs, and I'm going to suggest to you that this report, if you had an opportunity to read it, would be a balanced document for you to consider. And if you, Mr. Nort, go on, please, to page 18, the foot of, and then page 19. We see a reference to violations of --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this one case I'm supposed to decide that this is an impartial document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will, of course, have an opportunity to consider it at leisure if you can, but I just want to make it clear what I'm drawing to your attention. Now, here you'll see a reference to violations of due process. You were, of course, a traffic policeman. But if we go to page 19, we see a reference to Adem Bajri on the third paragraph. He was a Pec lawyer, wasn't he? You've told us how everybody knows everybody else in a small town. Adem Bajri was a Pec lawyer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you not know him? He was famous for defending those charged with what might be called political offences.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have to know him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know him and if you can't help us with what's said there, I'm going to move on. So that -- but so that we can understand it when we look at your documents, it goes this far, does it: No knowledge of criminal investigations, and now no knowledge of how the process of the courts operated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of knowledge can I have about that? You will probably ask me about specific judgements and decisions, and I know that courts of law operate on the basis of the law, and that is sufficient knowledge for me. As for specific cases and the lawyer Adem Bajri, they didn't really matter to me in my life. I had my own life and my own work. I don't need Human Rights Watch to establish for me what happened there, because I know for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him by name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. I read it here on the top of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go on to page 20, then, please, because there's a report here of the trial of the policemen, and you do have some recollection of that, and it says this -- towards the bottom of the page, please, Mr. Nort. Further down. That's fine. "In November and December 1994, 136 ethnic Albanians were arrested for forming a parallel Albanian police force. All of them were formerly Yugoslav policemen and were active in the police trade union." And I think you referred yourself, didn't you, to the police trade union when answering questions of this accused. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called themselves the trade union, but it was not a trade union. It was their illegal police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report goes on: "At various times during 1995, 117 of them were found guilty and sentenced to terms of imprisonment ranging from one to eight years. As of October 1996, some of them had been released." Do you remember that? Do you remember your former Albanian police colleagues, as they would have been, being tried, convicted and some of them being released?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know about them being tried and convicted or released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say in respect of these police defendants that Human Rights Watch, or Helsinki, spoke with the lawyers of the defendants and some of the defendants and suggests that torture was used to extract confessions. Is that the way things happened in your police station?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what happened in my police station and in police stations, rather, because I had several of them. So that did not happen in my police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you weren't the investigating officer, if you weren't present in the interview rooms, you have never been in charge of any investigation even of a household burglary, how are you able to tell us that these violent things didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That something happened in the buildings where I worked?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been hesitating to intervene because I expected a question to be put. However, since there's no question coming, I have to intervene now. Mr. Nice knows full well, because Investigating Judge Danica Marinkovic testified here and there were other witnesses, too, who spoke about laws. He would have to know that investigations are not carried out by policemen. They are carried out by investigating judges, and that's what Mr. Paponjak pointed out a few times as well. According to our law, it is the investigating judge who carries out an investigation. Mrs. Marinkovic explained here how she interviewed suspects in the presence of the prosecutor, the attorney for the suspect, and this is just witness badgering, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I see nothing improper about the question. The question was, "If you weren't the investigating officer, if you weren't present in the interviews rooms, how are you able to tell us that these violent things didn't happen?" It's for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just raise a matter. I've been holding my peace here, just listening with interest, because what's being put is that someone from Human Rights Watch has spoken to some defence lawyers who said that torture went on in the Pec police station. Well, if all cases were brought on what defence lawyers said happened on that basis without dealing with the real evidence, I think we'd probably be in a sorry state. I'm not really sure we're getting anywhere with this, because on the one hand the Prosecutor himself is just asserting the views and statements by people in a book who happen to be defence lawyers, and the witness is saying, "Well, I don't know about that," and really, the trial isn't being advanced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's trying to establish that the witness does not or did not have a sufficient factual basis for the evidence that he gave in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Neither does he, the Prosecutor. He's just reporting what defence lawyers said to someone that's in a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see nothing improper in the question. Let the witness answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether there was any torture in my police station, and my answer was no, there wasn't. The next question was how can I claim that? I can claim that because I never received such reports. This did not happen. Had something happened, I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, I'm going to deal with the accused's intervention where he says that under your legal system the investigating judge has the role of investigating. He's quite right. But we have had evidence from another area - Stimlje, near Racak - of how an officer, an investigating officer, can be charged with the business of taking statements from potential witnesses. Now, do you know that investigating officers take statements from potential witnesses, either on their own initiative or at the direction of an investigative judge? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do take statements on a number of grounds. One possibility is that it's required by the prosecutor or by the investigating judge or maybe when the citizen himself has something to say, but we are not investigators. We take statements as authorised officers of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there is either no right at all for people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interviewed to have a lawyer present with them, or alternatively, that it is simply the unvarying practice that if the police want to interview someone without a lawyer they can get away with it? What is the truth of those two, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An interview can take place without the presence of a lawyer if the citizen in question is not asking for a lawyer. If he does ask for a lawyer, then one is obtained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us make sure that things are properly understood. Mr. Nice noted that the witness was not a leading policeman on an investigating team, investigating a murder or something else. In this connection, I said that it is an investigating judge that leads an investigating team, which doesn't mean that policemen do not take part in any investigative action. But it is not true that a policeman can lead an investigation. The fact that he did never lead an investigation cannot be grounds for challenging that he has any knowledge about anything, including investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are hearing all the evidence, and we will assess it and determine what to credit and what not to credit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, I'm asking you these questions because when we come to 1999 and what happened when all the Kosovo Albanians left, you would accept, wouldn't you, that it's necessary to know the overall environment in which they lived, in which the Kosovo Albanians lived? It's necessary for us to know what was the overall environment, the nature of the overall environment in which they lived. You'd accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that very well because I lived together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm suggesting, which is why I'm going through this material, that the picture you have painted is grossly misleading and intentionally so, because you knew perfectly well, as you know now, throughout the 1990s and increasingly this was a police state, as allowed and ordered by this accused.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a question. I'm suggesting that's something that you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that I didn't know, it's that it's not true. I would like you to find one single Albanian who will find any objection to my work and who will say that he was discriminated against because he was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, were you aware of an attempt by Albanians to establish a parallel police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not attempt; they achieved it. We had information, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a simple answer. But you were not aware that a number had been arrested, prosecuted, and convicted, and indeed some acquitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of that, and I said I was aware of that. But as for convictions, I wasn't able to assist the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor asked me if I am aware of my colleagues who were convicted and released. But I did say that I was aware that some of them had been arrested on this charge, and that was in response to a question by the Prosecutor that was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The confusion may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I may have misunderstood this. You were aware of the case being taken against a large number, but 176 I think was the figure given, of policemen. You're aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This figure was read out. I don't know how many of them there were, but I know that the members of what was then the illegal MUP of the Republic of Kosovo had been arrested. I didn't know the number, the exact number. I didn't know their names. I didn't know the name of the investigating judge. I didn't know what the convictions were, and I didn't know that some of them were eventually released. But I know that things happened. I know about the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't -- the witness has answered the question, Mr. Milosevic. I'm content with that. If you want to raise the matter again, you can do it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just have a look at one entry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at one entry on the Human Rights Watch report for 1998, Exhibit 191. Just at page 54. This deals with part, in any event, of the 1998 story, or history. On page 54, that same lawyer, in 1998, Adem Bajri, is reported -- or reports that there were 251 ethnic Albanians in Pec gaol facing charges of terrorist activity, criminal charges having been filed against 510 others. And he reported -- now, that may be a thoroughly good thing if you've managed to find, or your police force managed to find 251 people against whom charges of terrorism could be laid. Were you aware of that number of terrorists being held, or alleged terrorists being held?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many were kept in prison, but we do have statistics for 1998, and we have them here. And we probably have a list of names to go with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive my inability to deal with the documents on account of their time of delivery and lack of translation. Can you tell us where we can find in your documents a reference to these 251 in gaol? Which schedule should we look to, or is this the work of someone else that you can't help us with? Can you help us? They're your documents, you see.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think an entire tab is dedicated to this. Chapter Z is the name I know it under. It contains specific data indicating names of people against whom criminal charges were filed. Two hundred fifty-one doesn't tell me anything. Maybe there are more, maybe there are less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things that is reported through Human Rights Watch is that this same lawyer alleged that -- and this is an allegation he made at the time, that nearly all his clients, and he represented many of them, 24, had been beaten in prison, had bruises to the body. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could confirm this, couldn't you: It's a dangerous job to be a human rights lawyer in Kosovo in the late 1990s, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I be able to confirm or deny it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know, of course, what happened to the most famous lawyer, Mr. Kelmendi, don't you? Everybody does. And his two sons. So it would be dangerous for this man to speak out publicly about what he says was happening to his clients. Do you not accept that it was dangerous in the late 1990s to pursue human rights interests in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that, because I was one of the people who was always advocating human rights. Are you saying that this was said secretly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The colonel just pointed out that it is in Chapter Z. It's to be found in Chapter Z. Those are tabs 9 and 9.1. They contain information about terrorists and terrorist organisations and the consequences of the terrorist activity in the area of the SUP of Pec from the 1st of January, 1998, to mid-2001. And as you can see, 1.170 incidents are recorded, including, I suppose, all the people who were arrested on this charge by the SUP of Pec. So if the witness says it's Chapter Z, that means it is to be found under tabs 9 and 9.1, including all the individual incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Mr. Nice, you will have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the documents have been translated, I will do my best to review them at the break. If they have not been translated, I'm not going to be able to do anything with them, but I am, of course, assisted by the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the next document I'm going to ask you to consider is again in English but it comes from a different source. It's a military situation report from the British dated May of 1998, and I'm just going to ask Mr. Nort to place it on the overhead projector. It's Exhibit 255. While it's coming your way, you would accept, wouldn't you -- you would accept, wouldn't you, that military representatives of various countries travelled in the region to try and see what was happening on the ground, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some of them occasionally, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this one reports the following: "Travelling from Pec to Decani when they were ambushed in one of the villages to the north of the checkpoint. One was killed and the other wounded." I'm sorry, I've got the wrong reference. Can I have it back, please. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we see on this report, we see at the foot of the page: "This morning we left Pec at 0736 and headed for Decani to see if we could get through. On leaving Pec the road was deserted. We soon came across spent cases --" 12.75 millimetre and other dimensions -- "on the road."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd better read it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This morning we left Pec at 0736 and headed for Decani to see if we could get through. On leaving Pec, the road was deserted. We soon came across spent cases ... 12.75 millimetres --" and other dimensions -- "on the road. Most of the buildings astride the main road in Ljubenic and Gorni --" and I'm sorry, I can't read all of that word -- "had been strafed. The spent cases had not been there more than a day or so. Some of the houses were burnt out. One in Gorni Streoc was still smouldering. The MUP was not in sight. The villages appeared deserted but after a short while a number of Albanian men came out to tell us what had happened. They said that the village had been attacked and 11 people were killed. The attacks took place on May the 25th. Their descriptions of the perpetrators match the JSO rather than the regular MUP." And they go on to give details. I save time by leaving it there. Now, an incident like this, close to your police station, must be one of which you were aware and must be one which you can remember, 11 people being killed. Can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to know if it's a real incident that has been reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like you to help us with is this: You've produced all these records. This is a major crime. Can you point me to any record that deals with it so that we can see how it was recorded at the time? Because this is 1998, you see, so I think we're in the period of your records, aren't we? Can you take me to the relevant record? Because I'm afraid I can't work my way round your documents very easily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which date in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date's given on the previous page, but I think it is -- it's Monday, the 25th of May is, I think, the date of the report, in 1998. Well, that's what -- indeed, that's what's said in the body of the report as the date for the attack, even if the Sitrep came a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point us to the place in your records if your records go back that far?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this Chapter A, you have reports on all incidents involving loss of life in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... right now, because A doesn't help me very much because we've got it tabbed under a different method. So we'll find it together. Where do I look? I'll get the index out. And what should be the heading for this, so that we can see how it was recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be headed "Brief for information on incidents involving loss of life." There should be an index of victims plus an index in the alphabetical order. We will easily find persons by alphabetical order, and we will easily find incidents by date, because they were also recorded listed chronologically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got -- it may be the quickest way: Do the documents have a Serbian language index at the beginning of tab 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, it is time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might the witness both take the index with him, because that will help us save time, and if he feels he can, might he write down the names of those who prepared the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may take the index, and if he can, then he can write down the names of those who prepared the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would like to use my break to rest, to have a cigarette and a coffee, if you allow me. If you don't allow me, I will continue to work during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, use the break to rest. And if you're -- use the break to rest if you wish. If you're in a position to do the exercise mentioned, then you can do the exercise, but I won't interfere with your rest. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't yet been able to track down the name of the policeman who was shot and killed, responsive to Judge Bonomy's question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, we're looking still at the document recording this very serious offence in Gorni Streoc. I shan't be able to conclude my examination today, unfortunately, therefore if you could -- sorry, that's too much. If you would, rather than go through the papers and take time now, unless you can point me immediately to the tab reference to that I'll ask you to find it overnight and to tell me where we can find it tomorrow. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is whether this question can be asked of the witness at all, because this document we still have on the ELMO says that a group of Albanians had come to those foreign representatives, and it says they said that "[In English] ... the group had been attacked and 11 people were killed." [Interpretation] That means they told the foreign representatives "[In English]... was wearing a set of an old-style ..." et cetera. "It was the same colour and contained several full AK47 magazines."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Raise this in re-examination, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you say about the description, Mr. Paponjak, from whenever it was, May 1998, of buildings damaged and burning the way described here. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it happened at all. And if it happened, I can't tell you how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it really your case that as the officer in charge of the traffic police, where you see a report from an international military observer describing things happening to buildings like this, you can't help us at all? That's really your position, is it? Or is it that you don't want to help us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My case is as follows: If that happened, it's in our documentation. In that case, I will be able to assist you. If it didn't happen, it's not on our records, and I can't comment on what didn't happen. That is the gist of what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 1998. Was there any reason of which you were aware why -- why international military observers - everybody was still hoping for resolution through peace at that time - would record things that were completely untrue? Is there any reason of which you're aware why that should happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said they put on record something that is not true. They recorded a story they heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at -- remember, if it's more difficult for you, you don't, of course, read the English, perhaps. They actually record houses being burnt out, you see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They actually record houses being burnt out. Why were houses being burnt out in May of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have been burnt by anybody. They could have been burned by terrorists, by some other people. And it's also possible that it was burned down by policemen. I believe that's what the author of this paper is trying to suggest. But if you ask me what I think, I think the houses were burned down by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Well, having no knowledge of it, which was your initial position, why do you think they were burned down by terrorists as opposed to by the policemen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because policemen didn't do such things. If somebody's burning down houses, then what can you call them except a terrorist?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 257 for a little later in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you give the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is 255, and the next one is 257.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just look at the bottom of the first page, you see this is the 5th and the 6th of August, and the reporting military observer says: "Most villages north or south of the Pec-Pristina road and Gornji Klina-Rudnik-Rakos road wantonly destroyed..." First of all, if the description is remotely accurate, wanton destruction of so much property, you must have been aware of it yourself. Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road Rudnik-Gornji Klina-Rakos was not within my jurisdiction. It's the area of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pec-Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pec-Pristina is a road that was within my jurisdiction, one section of it. Zenica was not, Junik was not, Jablanica, I don't know what is meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can you explain it to us? Because you will appreciate the suggestion is that this was Serb force work, terrorising the Albanian population. Now, you tell us: What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my understanding of this. This Pec-Pristina road was not damaged in any significant way in the section that we had under our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. control. I remember a period, though, where we were unable to -- when we were unable to control the road beyond Klina on towards Kosovska Mitrovica. We were able to control the Pec-Pristina road only up to Klina and only with great difficulty. The rest of the road was under the control of the terrorists, and it was blocked. The village of Kijevo was completely surrounded. That's all I know about that road. From Klina onwards, I know nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here is an incident of which you do know because you've already referred to it; the Salihaj family. How many of those were killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we recorded that as a killing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let's just deal with it in stages. You certainly know about it; you mentioned it in your evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in our documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a family of people, or a number of members of a family of people who were all killed. By whom were they killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would give me a moment to find this document here. It's the 9th of August, 1998, in a place called Susica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of August --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Susica is between Dubrava and -- we looked at it. It's close to Dubrava, isn't it? Don't you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know by heart but we have a map, we can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yourself, by the way, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there personally, neither at the moment when the terrorist attack happened nor for the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a terrorist attack or was it a revenge against the terrorist attack that led to all those people being killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clearly written here that a terrorist attack was carried out against the police patrol of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, that members of the police responded to fire, and on that occasion they killed eight members of the KLA. It doesn't say members of the Salihaj family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is your evidence that all eight were members of the KLA as opposed to perhaps just one?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a record of on-site investigation carried out by the investigating judge of the district court in Pec, and the rest of the documentation. There is the entire case file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's tab 1. Tab 1.4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 59. Tab 1.4, number 59 in the list of incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not been translated. I'll deal with it tomorrow and look at it overnight. We've heard evidence that -- from a witness called Crosland, that in the summer of 1998, Frenki Simatovic, commander of the Special Operations Unit, was in and around Pec. A senior policeman. Can you tell us what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know Mr. Simatovic. I never saw him there, and I can't tell you what he was doing there if he was there indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've had evidence from Lord Ashdown that on the 27th of September, in between then and the 28th of September of 1998, along the Pristina-Pec road, there was arson of property on a large scale. Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that. That, too, is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His evidence was to the effect that the houses seemed to have been burnt systematically, cattle had been killed. Is this road within your traffic duty area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which villages he spoke of. So if you give me the name of a village or a place along that road, I would be able to tell you whether we controlled it or not or whether it was the SUP of Pristina that controlled it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... area of Klina are in your jurisdiction, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of responsibility, but not under control. Some. I don't know who you're referring to, which ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we going to be able to find in the documents that you brought here, if we can read them, account of the burning, the trashing, as Lord Ashdown described it, I think, of houses in that area on those last days of September of 1998? Are we?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you just off the top of my head whether we would find them. I can take a look to see if there were any during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps again if you find the time you'll do it overnight because I don't want to weary the Judges with waiting time rather than use it. Waiting or wasting time. Can we move now, then, please, to the presence of paramilitaries operating in your area. Do you know about somebody called Srecko Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name doesn't seem familiar at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Zvonimir Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a man by the name of Zvonimir Cvetkovic from Pec because he's the brother of an employee of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the man who died in 1999, Zvonimir Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't die in 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you'd just like to have a look at this. "Under Orders" is Exhibit 145. And if Mr. Nort could show that page to the witness, and then display that page on the overhead projector. First show the page to the witness. You're looking at a memorial there. Do you remember that memorial? That is memorial to the man Cvetkovic, described as "The last salute from colleagues and officers from the OPG and PJP units, the Pec police department."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what I'm looking at, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I see the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the memorial being erected to this man Cvetkovic? I mean, you were number two in the police effectively. I mean there were several of you at the same level. Do you not remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the number two in the Pec police at the time; and secondly, I'm not quite clear on what this document is. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there an actual picture of the memorial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn over the page, please, and display that. That's it, I think.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two quite different people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. That's Budimir -- yes. Could we go back to the previous page, then, please. Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Zvonimir Cvetkovic, whom I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in a company called Petrans, that is to say a transport company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now look at the left-hand page, please, Mr. Nort. And can we have the picture at the bottom, the caption at the bottom. Could you move it up, please. Thank you. This photograph shows a man identified as Zvonimir Cvetkovic with a group of unidentified men at the Petrans trucking company in Pec, Kosovo, where he worked. He was seen with Serbian security forces on May 14 in Cuska when 41 ethnic Albanian men were executed. Was he investigated for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people in the photograph are not members of the security force. None of the people here. They don't belong to either the police or the army. This is Zvonimir Cvetkovic, and he is the one next to the truck here in this photograph, to my right, on the far right. As to the other men there, I don't know them, but I can say with certainty that they weren't members of either the police force or the SUP of Pec because I knew all the members personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So none of these people here were in the security forces. Quite possibly these were colleagues from the company he worked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through this exhibit, which is available, in any great detail, but it makes the point, or suggests, that for Pec there were several photographs of people identified as serious offenders. Here is one, a man known to you. You've shown us records of investigations, you've told us it was your duty to investigate crimes wherever the information came from. Was this man investigated for the crime alleged here to which he was connected? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who is giving that information, what the source is of that information. I didn't have it available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I have the book back, please, Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on in order to leave only a few topics, if I can, for tomorrow morning. I want to turn to -- back to aspects of Dubrava prison because I want your answers tonight rather than tomorrow morning in relation to matters that we may be able to deal with rapidly on the video. Your visits, you told us today, were on the 19th, the 25th, and you then said after the on-site visit of the 21st. Let's deal with them in order. On the first visit on the 19th, did you make notes yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in my working notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that available here?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My notebooks are rather big ones, and I couldn't bring them here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went -- did you go round with the people making the video?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I arrived before them on the site on the 19th. I was close by. And as soon as we received information and the bombing ceased, we went on location, and several people who were with me went as well. And when I approached the site, a van with the wounded was moving towards Istok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is it you're able to tell us, if anything, about the video that reflects the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is this: I can tell you who filmed the videotape and that it was filmed by members of the crime technician department of the SUP of Pec crime department when they went to do the on-site investigation, and that the investigation on that particular day, the 19th of May, was headed by the investigating judge of the district court of Istok with the presence of the president of the district court of Pec. That's what I can tell you about that particular videotape and that it is an official material, an official document of the SUP of Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies were found on that day in the rubble?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three bodies were found that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't challenge that. We can move on to the next date chronologically. On the 21st, you arrived at what time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I was in Dubrava on the 21st. I saw the investigation on-site crew on the premises of the Istok Ministry of the Interior after the bombing at Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must have misunderstood your answer. So what, if anything, are you able to tell us about the, I think, comparatively small part of the video that appears to be dated the 21st of May? Can you tell us anything or nothing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long that footage is. It was shown fast forwarded here. As far as I recall, what can be seen is the destruction and the journalists going there and some other details. I can't remember them all now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it shows no more bodies, does it, that footage? It only shows damage to buildings.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could probably see the bombings had there not been the bombing. They didn't succeed in completing the on-site investigation because while they were doing that the planes began flying overhead and the prison was bombed again. And the investigating judge notes in his minutes, in the records, that that's what happened, that the bombing started and that they all left the site as soon as possible without having completed their on-site investigation. Had they done so, they probably would have filmed the bodies as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What material do you point to that shows us the last occasion of bombing by NATO at Dubrava prison? What's the bit of material or evidence or document that shows us the last moment of bombing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the video footage, you cannot see the bombing at any point. The video footage was done after the bombing every time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I want you to help us if you can: When did NATO last bomb Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to help you by telling you what I know. Now, I cannot even give you a rough estimate of when NATO last bombed Dubrava. However, I'm sure you'd be able to find it in the information and report that was compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, NATO acknowledged in press briefings and also in a letter, if anybody wants to see it, bombing on the 19th and the 21st of May. Can you point to any piece of material that suggests there was any bombing after maybe the night of the 21st of May, but any time after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are the minutes, the records kept by the investigating judge, the judge's notes, and the notes of authorised individuals as well as our own notes. And my own working notebook, in fact, where I'm sure one would be able to find that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date does this material show?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which material?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the material you've just listed. You're coming here to speak, there's a body of material --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and I want you to tell us what's the last date of bombing.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material indicates the dates that are stipulated in the information drawn up on the basis of that material, the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be of assistance. Tab 46, for instance, point 3, of the Official Note of the Investigating Judge Vladan Bojic, the last paragraph says the following: It says that the NATO bombing was continued on the same day from 17 to 1705 [as interpreted] and 23 hours -- 2310 hours [as interpreted], and then on the following day, the 22nd of May, from 0610 hours. That's what it says in this particular document. And I provide that document in tab 46.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must find tab 46.3 now to see what it does say. And, if anything shows the difficulty of working with untranslated documents, this exercise does, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This one's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last binder, 7. I remember I asked some questions on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage that we have, then, this comes from -- is dated the 22nd of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It looks like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, if we look at this document, which the accused has read out in part, it comes from the Investigative Judge Bojic, and it goes no further than to suggest that bombs were dropped at 23.15 on the night of the 21st, and it suggests at 6.10 on the morning of the 22nd. Apart from this document, do you have any other material to show bombing after the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the practice for us to ask the investigating judge to give us the material that he had compiled if he had happened to write anything down. That's the first point. Secondly, we all have in our working notebooks the exact record of the time when each person saw the bombing take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So most people recorded this. Now, I haven't brought that material with me here because I didn't know it would be necessary. I considered that it would be sufficient to have the records written by the investigating judge. We didn't do this to use documents before this Tribunal. We compiled them for our own needs and requirements. That is why the material is lacking in terms of what you expect to find here, but we compiled it for our own purposes and that was sufficient. We have what we need to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if the investigating judge's report was accurate, then whoever prepared the information on Dubrava bombing would have recorded that there was bombing on the 23rd of May -- the 22nd of May; is that correct? They must have done.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take tab 8, please. Who prepared this one? This is the summary on Dubrava prison.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled by the same working group working on the whole documentation, on all the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... point me to an individual who is going to bear responsibility for the contents of this document, apart from yourself.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd use the term "who compiled." I don't think you can say responsible. That individual does not bear responsibility. But it says here that the NATO Air Force, on the 22nd, at about 6.00, launched an attack using a number of projectiles, in this piece of information, on the 22nd of May at 6.10 hours. That is page 2, third paragraph from the top, you will find that there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A reflection of the judge's contribution. And it identifies the buildings hit, doesn't it? The compound was hit, the boiler room, the motel, administration building, motor pool, and almost the entire infrastructure. And it makes it clear in the following paragraph that there was no bombing on the 23rd, because on the 23rd NATO overflew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 3 in the English. Last page in the English. So sorry. Second to last page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only indication in mine of bombing on the 24th is the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. We'll come back to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we not get there quite quickly? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if you look at the body of the document, Mr. Paponjak, it's clear that no allegation of bombing after 6.10 on the 22nd is made, the 23rd is overflight, but the title of the document, as His Honour Judge Bonomy observes, suggests there was bombing on the 24th. You actually have no evidence of bombing after the 22nd at 6.10 a.m., do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a matter of interest, can you explain why it's suggested in the title that there was bombing on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation for that. Maybe the date was typed out incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went there on this day. Not on -- on the date of the second filming, the 22nd, did you? I can't remember now. Which date did you go on? The 25th you went, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by that time, the bodies were all lined up where?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't go to the prison at all on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't in the prison. On the 25th I was at the cemetery, at the cemetery when the bodies were -- had already been prepared for burial, and that's the location I was at, and I said that I remember that day very well because there were a large number of bodies, it was very hot weather, and the people were going about their business. I stayed for maybe half an hour and returned. That means that on the 25th I was at the cemetery during just one stage of the work that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what we know is that some of the bodies had labels on them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the labels gave names.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were numbers, labels with numbers. That's what I saw when I was there. So what I saw on that particular day was that the bodies had been labelled with numbers and that holes were being dug to bury those bodies. I didn't attend the burial until the end. I might have stayed for just half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of them, because the accused drew our attention to one this morning, had names on them as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of them --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll look at these tomorrow. Some of them had the dates upon which they were said to have died. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to details like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because on the material produced, even at tab 8's highest, there could be no justification for writing on a body that the person had died on the 23rd or been killed on the 23rd, could there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean killed by bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or in any other way. Killed by bombing, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There could be no explanation for somebody being shown to have been killed by bombing on the 23rd, because your own report makes it clear that the last moment of bombing, so said, was at 6.10 on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who did write that. What I saw when we stopped the film appeared to me to be something that was written by somebody other than members of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prisoners wrote their own names -- or not their own names. They wrote the names of those whom they knew, didn't they? That's how they were identified.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know, but that was written by an Albanian. If we look at the footage, we'll see that and I'll explain to you why I say that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've tried to suggest, or the accused has tried to suggest through you that those of the Dubrava victims who were found to have died through gunshot may have died running away. You have absolutely no evidence of that of any kind, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said had happened. I didn't claim that. All I claimed was that that possibility existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you claim that the possibility exists, will you now please confirm that you have not one scrap of evidence to support such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed that that's what happened for me to be -- for me to have to provide evidence to back it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
